title: Beyond Replacement: A Recursive Framework for NAMs, Animal Models, and Translational Neuroscience
content: A persistent problem in translational neuroscience is that increasingly detailed molecular and cellular findings often fail to produce meaningful improvements in human behavior or function. We argue that part of this problem comes from the way therapeutic development is organized. Translation is still often treated as a progression from molecular target to cellular model to animal model to human study. That sequence is useful for some questions, but it can obscure the experimental reality that evidence at one level of biology does not automatically predict what will happen at another. We propose a recursive framework that begins with a clearly defined functional or behavioral domain. Human data and computational methods are then used to identify heterogeneity and generate testable hypotheses. Human-derived new approach methodologies (NAMs), including induced pluripotent stem cell models and organoids, are used to test cellular and developmental mechanisms. Animal models are used selectively when the question requires intact physiology, circuit integration, environmental interaction, or behavior. Results at each stage can revise the assumptions made at earlier stages. This framework changes the role of both NAMs and animal models. Validated NAMs can replace animal experiments for defined questions within their demonstrated capabilities. We propose that their use to resolve cellular and developmental questions before in vivo testing could reduce poorly targeted animal experiments and focus remaining studies. We argue that this approach provides a practical way to apply Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement (the 3Rs) according to the scientific question being asked rather than treating replacement as the only measure of progress.
